newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Snap up gilts for post-election profit.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Snap up gilts for post-election profit.

text.p: Yield hungry investors looking for medium term gains sheltered from volatile markets in Europe, should snap up British gilts, analysts said on Wednesday.

A 10-year gilt/Bund yield spread of around 180 basis points was a buying opportunity, they said. Political risk after the looming election will dwindle, squeezing spreads up to 20 basis points in the next four months or so.
"A spread of 180 basis points is a fairly attractive level to buy gilts against Bunds for a longer term hold," said Societe Generale gilts analyst Tom Rayner.
"You may get hit by volatility before the election, but if you're prepared to ride that, I think 180 is attractive."
Rayner said he expected the spread to narrow to around 160 basis points within one to two months after the election. By 1217 GMT the 10-year gilt/Bund spread was at 176 basis points.
The present Conservative government must call an election by the end of May, with May 1 thought to be the favoured date by Prime Minister John Major.
The government faces an uphill task to get re-elected, with the opposition Labour party enjoying around a 20 point lead in opinion polls.
Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW, was even more optimistic about gilts' performance in the next few months.
"If you think inflation is benign over the next few months, that public borrowing is OK and we get a change of government ...all that could contribute to pushing the spread in," he said.
Adams said the 10-year gilt/Bund spread could narrow to 100 to 125 basis points by the middle of the year.
He said gilts were relatively protected from last week's rout in peripheral European bond markets.
"That should help to drive home to international investors that the UK is a safe haven," he said.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke was widely expected to leave interest rates on hold following his regular monthly meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George on Wednesday.
But this would do little to dispell the optimism about gilts, said analysts.
While only time will tell whether Clarke has fallen behind the curve in a bid to spare the electorate unpopular interest rate rises, they said recent data supported his decision.

"It's quite reasonable for Clarke to take the attitude at the moment that there are uncertainties in the economy so he's happy to stave off a rate rise," said Adams. "And he won't risk getting too far behind the curve as a result of that."

Ifty Islam, European bond strategist at Merrill Lynch, agreed above 180 basis points was an attractive gilt/Bund spread, but added he would advise taking profits at around 170 basis points before the election.
"Traders generally have to be a bit lighter on their feet, as liquidity will dry up going into an election cycle and investors will not want to pick too many aggresive plays in the market," he said.
"Whereas previously we might have looked for a move to 160 basis points, that now looks a bit ambitious ahead of the election."
But he added on a six to 12 month view the spread could narrow to 130 basis points.
Analysts agreed the gilt yield curve would flatten after the election, but added this was largely anticipated by the market and would not prompt too big a sell-off at the longer end.
